title: Structured Sober Living
desc: A furnished room in a drug and alcohol free house, with curfews, chores and check-ins that give the week a shape you can rely on.
subtitle: A drug and alcohol free house with a routine you can lean on while the rest of life steadies.
intro: Every house runs on the same few rules: no substances on site, a curfew that everyone keeps, chores that rotate weekly, and random testing. The rules are not there to catch people out. They are there so that nobody has to rely on willpower alone at eleven at night.
Rooms are furnished and bedding is provided. You arrive with your things and a place to put them, and the first week is mostly about sleep, meals at regular times and learning how the house works.
bullets: A curfew that is the same for everyone in the house
Chores on a rota, swapped out each week
Random drug and alcohol testing
An evening check-in with staff or the house lead
section: Sober living works best for people coming out of detox or residential treatment who are not ready to go straight back to an old address. It also suits anyone whose home situation makes staying sober harder than it needs to be.
You do not need to have everything worked out before you move in. Most residents arrive with a bag, a phone and a lot of uncertainty, and build the rest from here.

focus.title: Safe and sober
focus.text: Substance free housing with testing and clear consequences, so the house stays a place people can trust.

focus.title: Steady routine
focus.text: Regular meals, curfews and chores that rebuild the ordinary rhythm addiction tends to flatten.

title: Peer Support Groups
desc: House meetings and peer groups every week, where residents talk honestly about what is working and what is not.
subtitle: Weekly groups where residents speak plainly about the week they have actually had.
intro: The house meets once a week, everyone in the same room. Residents raise what is on their mind: a difficult shift, a family call that went badly, a craving that came out of nowhere. Nobody is required to perform progress.
Smaller peer groups run alongside the house meeting. These are led by residents further along in recovery, with staff nearby rather than in charge.
bullets: One whole-house meeting each week, attendance expected
Smaller peer groups led by longer-term residents
What is said in the room stays in the room
Outside fellowship meetings supported and encouraged
section: Advice from someone who has been in the same chair six months earlier lands differently. Peers notice the things staff miss, and they are harder to deflect with a polite answer.
Over time most residents find themselves on the other side of that exchange, which turns out to be one of the steadier parts of staying well.

focus.title: Honest rooms
focus.text: Groups built on the understanding that nobody has to pretend the week went better than it did.

focus.title: Shared load
focus.text: Early recovery carried between people instead of alone in a quiet room.

title: Key Worker Sessions
desc: One to one time with a key worker to set goals, sort out paperwork and keep the practical side of recovery moving.
subtitle: Regular one to one time with someone whose job is to keep your plan moving.
intro: Every resident is matched with a key worker in their first week. You meet regularly, agree what the next few weeks need to look like, and review it honestly rather than tidily.
Sessions cover the unglamorous parts of recovery: appointments, benefits, debt letters, court dates, a GP who needs chasing. These are the things that quietly sink people when nobody helps.
bullets: Goals set with you, reviewed on a schedule
Appointments, paperwork and referrals
Relapse prevention planning, written down
A move-on plan, started early rather than late
section: Key workers are not counsellors and do not pretend to be. Where therapy is needed we refer, and we keep working alongside whoever provides it.
If something goes wrong, the session is still the place to say so. Residents who tell their key worker early almost always come through it better than those who wait.

focus.title: One person who knows
focus.text: A named key worker who knows your situation without you starting from scratch each time.

focus.title: Written plans
focus.text: Goals and relapse plans on paper, so progress is something you can actually check.

title: Work and Study Support
desc: Help with CVs, interviews, benefits and getting back into training, so that your days fill up with something steady.
subtitle: Practical help getting back into work, training or study at a pace that holds.
intro: Empty days are hard to survive in early recovery. Work gives structure, money and a reason to be somewhere, so we start on it sooner than most people expect.
That means CVs, applications and interview practice, and honest conversations about gaps in your history and how to talk about them.
bullets: CVs, applications and interview practice
Explaining gaps and convictions without apology or oversharing
Benefits, ID documents and bank accounts
Courses, apprenticeships and return-to-study routes
section: Full time work in week two is rarely the win it looks like. We would rather start with a few shifts, a course or volunteering and build from there.
Residents in work keep their house responsibilities. Meetings and check-ins move around shifts, but they do not disappear.

focus.title: Something to do
focus.text: Days with a shape to them, which protects recovery better than any amount of good intention.

focus.title: Money sorted
focus.text: Benefits, ID and bank accounts straightened out, so the basics stop being a crisis.

title: Family Reconnection
desc: Guided visits and family sessions, at the pace that suits everyone involved, to rebuild trust that took a hit.
subtitle: Rebuilding family trust slowly, with support on both sides of the conversation.
intro: Addiction damages the people around it, and recovery does not repair that automatically. Families often arrive hopeful and exhausted in equal measure.
We support contact at a pace everyone can manage: a phone call before a visit, a short visit before a day out, and nobody pushed into a reunion they are not ready for.
bullets: Guided visits in a setting that suits everyone
Family sessions with a worker present
Honest guidance for relatives on what helps and what does not
Support around contact with children, alongside any formal arrangements
section: Trust comes back through small kept promises, not big speeches. A visit that happens when it was supposed to happen does more than any apology.
Where relationships cannot be repaired, we help residents accept that without treating it as a failure of recovery.

focus.title: Both sides supported
focus.text: Families get guidance too, rather than being left to guess what helps.

focus.title: No forced timelines
focus.text: Contact moves at the pace the slowest person in the room can manage.

title: Aftercare and Alumni
desc: Support does not stop at move-out. Alumni keep their place at house meetings and mentor residents coming up behind them.
subtitle: The support carries on after you move out, in both directions.
intro: Moving on is the point of sober living, and it is also the moment people are most exposed. Aftercare exists so that the drop is a step rather than a cliff.
Alumni keep a standing invitation to the weekly house meeting, and many take up mentoring a newer resident once they are steady.
bullets: A standing place at the weekly house meeting
Check-in calls in the first months after moving out
Mentoring, once you are ready to offer it
A route back if things wobble, without shame attached
section: Alumni events keep the connection ordinary rather than ceremonial: a meal, a walk, a Sunday morning meeting people turn up to because they want to.
Residents who mentor usually say it does as much for them as for the person they are mentoring. Explaining why the rules matter is a good way of remembering it yourself.

focus.title: A soft landing
focus.text: Check-ins and a standing invitation, so moving out is not the end of the support.

focus.title: A way back
focus.text: If things slip, the door is open and the conversation starts without judgement.
